analysis.one_liner: Strips tax breaks from billionaire-scale landlords, taxes their home sales, and cuts off their mortgage backing.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2026 with 17 Democratic cosponsors, the bill has sat in two House committees without a markup or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets large investors — anyone with more than $100 million in assets — who own single-family homes. It would take away their deductions for mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation on existing homes, charge them a tax equal to the full sale price of any home they sell, and bar Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae from buying, guaranteeing, or securitizing their mortgages. Money raised would go into the Housing Trust Fund for affordable rental housing. New construction and a landlord's own residence are exempt. The goal is to make it unprofitable for Wall Street-scale investors to hold homes that families might buy and to divert some money toward low-income housing.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and first-time homebuyers competing against deep-pocketed investors for existing homes would benefit if the bill makes corporate ownership of houses unprofitable and pushes those homes back onto the market. Extremely low- and very low-income families, including homeless families, would gain through Housing Trust Fund spending paid for by the new excise tax. Homeowners in neighborhoods where large investors have bid up prices could also see less price pressure.

how_it_helps.text: Ending deductions for mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation makes leveraged ownership of existing homes more expensive for firms with more than $100 million in assets, reducing the tax-advantaged edge they hold over family buyers.
The 100% excise tax on any home such an investor sells pushes big landlords toward selling off their portfolios, which would return homes to the market where individual buyers can reach them.
Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae could no longer buy, guarantee, or securitize mortgages made to these large investors, removing a federal subsidy from corporate single-family rental deals.
Money collected under the bill goes to the Housing Trust Fund, which funds rental housing affordable to extremely low- and very low-income families, including homeless families.

analysis.who_pays: Large investors — firms and wealthy individuals with over $100 million in assets that own single-family rentals — would pay through lost deductions, a 100% excise tax on home sales, and loss of access to Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae mortgage backing. Some tenants in investor-owned homes could face rent increases or, in a rapid sell-off scenario, short-term disruption.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax equals the full sale price of any home a large investor sells, which functions as a near-total ban on selling and could invite legal challenges or disorderly fire-sale exits rather than an orderly pullback.

Removing mortgage interest and depreciation deductions would raise these landlords' costs of ownership, and some of that could be passed to tenants as higher rents, at least until investors exit the market.

The $100 million threshold applies to any person's total assets, so it reaches wealthy individual landlords and family offices that own even a handful of homes, not only large institutional investors.

Money collected goes to the Housing Trust Fund, but the bill only allows its use 'to the extent provided for in advance in appropriations Acts' — future Congresses would have to actually appropriate it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim — ending taxpayer-subsidized borrowing and federal mortgage backing for billionaire-scale landlords — targets a small group and could lower prices for buyers and slow investor-driven rent pressure. But the design is blunt: an excise tax equal to the entire sale price is a near-total prohibition rather than a calibrated penalty, which invites litigation and could force disorderly sell-offs, and the $100 million asset threshold reaches individual wealthy landlords, not just Wall Street firms. If large investors retrenched faster than new supply came online, some markets could see tighter rental options. The help for low-income renters depends on Congress actually appropriating the collected money.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits with the House Ways and Means and Financial Services Committees, which have taken no action on it since it was referred to them the day it was introduced.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna and 14 House colleagues introduced the bill on January 16, 2026.
The Speaker referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means and to the Committee on Financial Services the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history after the referral.
The bill has 17 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, large corporate landlords are untouched: the bill has not advanced far enough to affect anyone, and the concentrated interests it targets bear no cost from its inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporate landlords, untouched so far

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and both committees of referral are chaired by Republicans, so the bill's fate rests entirely with the House majority.

industries.industry: Large single-family rental investors (REITs and firms with over $100M in assets)
industries.note: They would lose mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation deductions on existing homes, face a tax equal to the full sale price on any home they sell, and lose access to Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae mortgage backing. Their profits depend on buying homes that families would otherwise bid on and charging tenants rent, so their loss in this bill is the public's gain.

industries.industry: Mortgage finance and securitization (banks and issuers serving large landlords)
industries.note: The bill bars the housing finance enterprises from newly purchasing or securitizing mortgages made to specified large investors, cutting off a lending channel. That business exists to finance corporate home buying, so its interest runs against the bill's housing goals.

The bill exempts homes originally constructed or substantially rehabilitated by the taxpayer, so large investors could keep buying newly built homes from builders. Builders keep a major customer pool while competitors reselling existing homes are squeezed.

analysis.trajectory: With 17 cosponsors out of 217 House Democrats, no Republican support, and a dual referral to two Republican-chaired committees that have taken no action since January, the bill is very likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress without ever reaching a vote.
